title: Yama gives Nachiketa one word
hookLine: a boy turns down every treasure Death offers and gets a single syllable instead; Patanjali tells how to use it
carry: japa: say the name, and mean it
tomorrow: a king sets out to become a sage, and slips. then what?
last: ISHVARA PRANIDHANA — MET FROM THE OTHER SIDE.

cards: You know Nachiketa: the boy who waited three days at Death's door. Yama, lord of death, offers him three wishes to make up for it, and for the third the boy asks what happens after we die.
Yama tries to buy him off: long life, herds, gold, music, chariots. Nachiketa says keep them. And in the Katha Upanishad, Death, impressed, begins to teach.
Among the first things he gives the boy isn't a treasure at all. It's one word.

teach.h: THE WORD ALL THE VEDAS PRAISE: OM.
teach.b: Yama says, in paraphrase: the word every Veda praises, the word all austerity is for, the reason students live their disciplined lives, I'll tell you briefly. It is om. This syllable is Brahman; it is the highest.
Centuries later Patanjali picks up the same syllable and gives it three sutras, crisp as a recipe. Sutra 1.27: tasya vachakah pranavah.
The word that expresses Ishvara, yesterday's Lord, is the pranava, the old name for om. Vyasa adds that the bond between this word and the Lord isn't made up; using the word reveals it.
Sutra 1.28: taj japas tad artha bhavanam.
Its repetition, and dwelling on its meaning. Japa: saying it again and again. Artha bhavana: letting the meaning soak in as you say it.

Sutra 1.29: from that, awareness turns inward and the obstacles fall away. This is the teaching under a practice found in many Hindu homes: japa, a divine name repeated, often on a mala, a string of beads.
And the sutra's point is that the sound alone isn't the whole of it. Yama didn't give Nachiketa a noise; he gave him a word with Brahman inside it.
Many Hindu teachers say the same holds for any name of God a person loves: Rama, Krishna, Shiva.

teach.h: SAY THE NAME, AND MEAN IT.
teach.b: Today, it's the difference between counting beads while planning your week, and saying the name like you mean it.

how: Many Hindus repeat om or a divine name in japa, often on a mala, a string of beads, and teachers stress that the repetition should be joined with attention to the name's meaning, as Yoga Sutra 1.28 describes.

o: om, the humming syllable that names the Lord
a long hymn of praise sung at the dawn rite
a breath held long in the pause between chants

games.q: Death's gift, and the recipe for using it.
p: gives him om, the word the Vedas praise
repeating the name again and again

s: Patanjali says repeating om alone, without its meaning, is enough
1.28 pairs repetition with dwelling on the meaning.
in the Katha Upanishad, Yama tells Nachiketa the word all the Vedas praise is om
pranava is an old name for om
1.27: the pranava is the word that expresses Ishvara.

games.q: you've been chanting om for weeks, but it's become background noise. what does sutra 1.28 suggest?
o: join the sound with its meaning: dwell on what it names.
games.why: taj japas tad artha bhavanam: its repetition, and dwelling on its meaning. Yama gave Nachiketa a word with Brahman inside; the two belong together.

practice: If you have a mala, hold it; if not, use your fingers. On each out-breath, let om sound, aloud or silently: that's japa. After a few rounds, let it carry meaning, the Lord, Brahman, the whole, as you understand it.
If om isn't your word, use a name of God you love; if you don't pray, a word for what you hold highest. Again and again, the sound full instead of empty.

wordCard.voice: Pranava, the old name for om. Sutra 1.27: this word expresses Ishvara. Yama gave it to Nachiketa; Patanjali says repeat it, and dwell on its meaning.

orig.note: Sanskrit praṇava: an old name for om. in 1.27, the word that expresses Ishvara.

carryVoice: Your line: japa, say the name, and mean it. Sound and meaning, held together each time. See you tomorrow.
